script: We reverse gazumped a greedy landlord and it was glorious.. Gazumping happens when an agent or seller accepts an offer you make to buy a property at an agreed price but the property is sold to someone else. This usually happens when the vendor sells the place for a higher amount. This happened 15 years ago and it's one of the proudest moments of my life. My bestie and her hubby had five kids—like, a full-on squad. They were living in a pricey city, paying $400 a week for an old four‑bedroom that looked like it'd been abandoned for a decade. The kitchen was a horror show, drains smelled like a sewer, and every time you opened a window you felt the whole block's vibe. But hey, it was the only place they could afford, so they made it work. The owner was an elderly lady, rich as hell, who was super sweet to my bestie. She froze the rent for five years and promised that once we saved enough to get a bank loan, we could buy the house. She'd done it for other people too, so trust was there. We saved every penny, cut out snacks, and after five long years we told her we were ready. Two days later, the old lady passed away—no paperwork, no formalities, just a funeral. Enter the new owners: her four kids, each a millionaire with a portfolio of properties. They called us and said the sale would still happen but we'd have to wait for probate. We were confident, so we started fixing the place. We stripped wallpaper, painted, and mapped out future renovations. Finally probate cleared, and they agreed to sell at the previously agreed price. We applied for a loan. To our shock, it got denied. The kids had secretly raised the asking price by $80,000 and put the house on the open market. In seven days there'd be an open house, and with the market how it was, it'd sell fast. I was devastated. My friends might get the loan, but it would take longer than a week. Meanwhile, property prices were soaring, rents had jumped, and they'd been stuck at $400. If the house sold to someone else, they'd be evicted or face a higher rent—hard to find an affordable two‑bedroom. I was scared for them, but I was also incinerated with anger. Those rich kids were just screwing over a struggling family for less than $20,000 each. They didn't need the money. It was pure greed, and it was obvious they'd planned this. So while they scrambled to get cash, I plotted. I Googled what makes a house look bad without making us look like bad tenants. First step: clutter. We moved all furniture into the walls, added extra pieces, borrowed ornaments, and hung a pile of motorcycle memorabilia on the walls. The place looked cramped, like a museum of junk. Second: smell. I boiled a head of cabbage on the stove and sprayed ammonia around the front and back doors—because the neighborhood cats had been marking their territory, you know? Then we dropped two dozen rotten eggs down the drain to create a sewer‑gas vibe. Yikes. Third: neighbor sabotage. We got a moldy couch and dumped it in the front yard of the neighbor across the road—permission, of course. We also called friends with loud, crappy cars. They did a few laps in front of the block during the open day. The street was unusually busy that day. Everyone we knew had a reason to drive by, like rush hour. Fourth: rugby club. We called out mates from the rugby club—full‑contact, no padding. Most were big guys. The next door neighbor set up a BBQ, we offered free food and cheap beer. They came on motorcycles, wearing their roughest gear. Crowd was intense. All these distractions turned the open day into a circus. People came, some stayed for a minute, And that's how it all went down.
